mainTopic: Lashes and payment together: the source that one pays and is not flogged, and ריש לקיש's view that our משנה follows רבי מאיר, who holds both apply.
overview: The גמרא is trying to show that someone liable for both lashes and money pays and is not flogged. It first finishes testing the proof from the men who fight and hit a pregnant woman. רב סמא explains that court lashes, which have a limit, are lighter than death, so a warning for death still covers lashes. Then רב יעקב מנהר פקוד shows that this proof does not work for רבי. In the name of רבא, he brings a new source from the פסוק of one who strikes his fellow: the attacker was warned for death, yet the תורה makes him pay שבת and ריפוי. רב אשי's challenge that lashes may be worse than death is answered (his question whether a warning for a severe matter covers a lighter one gets no explicit answer), but רב מרי's challenge, that the פסוק may be about an accident, is left as a קשיא. ריש לקיש then gives a different answer: our משנה follows רבי מאיר, who holds a person is lashed and also pays. To defend this, the גמרא explains that a ברייתא where רבי מאיר seems to hold 'dies and pays' is about a thief whose agent slaughtered. That leads to the question of why the חכמים exempt the thief, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Maybe lashes are worse than death
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי, continuing his challenge from the previous amud, questions the assumption that death is the more severe punishment. He brings רב's statement that lashes would have broken חנניה, מישאל, and עזריה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps lashes are more severe? As רב said: had they flogged חנניה, מישאל, and עזריה, they would have bowed to the idol!
steps.whatsHappening: This continues רב אשי's challenge to the proof from the fighting men, which began on the previous amud. Even granting that a warning for a severe matter covers a lighter one, maybe lashes, not death, are the harsher punishment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier proof assumed death is the 'severe matter' and lashes the 'light matter.' If lashes are really harsher, a warning about death does not cover lashes. Then the proof that he pays instead of getting lashes falls apart. רב's statement supports this: those three צדיקים chose the fiery furnace, but lashes might have broken them.

keyTerms.meaning: They would have worshipped the idol

phrases.english: Perhaps lashes are more severe?
As Rav said:
Had they flogged Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah —
phrases.notes: Instead of throwing them into the fiery furnace (דניאל פרק ג).

phrases.english: they would have worshipped the idol!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the earlier proof that a warning for death covers lashes.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption that death is more severe than lashes.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If lashes are harsher than death, a warning about death does not automatically include a warning about lashes.

steps.title: Limited lashes versus unlimited beating
steps.stepSummary: רב סמא answers that רב was talking about endless beating. Court lashes have a fixed limit and are lighter than death.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב סמא son of רב אסי (some say son of רב אשי) said to רב אשי: Don't you see a difference between beating that has a limit and beating that has no limit?
steps.whatsHappening: The challenge is answered: רב's statement was about torture with no end. The מלקות of a בית דין has a set limit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Beating with no limit, meant to force someone to give in, can be worse than death. תורה lashes have a fixed number, so they stay lighter than death. That means death is still the 'severe matter,' and the earlier proof stands.

keyTerms.meaning: A fixed limit or set amount
And some say (another version of who said it)

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב סַמָּא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אַסִּי לְרַב אָשֵׁי,
phrases.english: Rav Samma, son of Rav Asi, said to Rav Ashi,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ רַב סַמָּא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אָשֵׁי לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: and some say it was Rav Samma, son of Rav Ashi, to Rav Ashi:
And is there no difference to you
between beating that has a limit
and beating that has no limit?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלָא שָׁנֵי לָךְ בֵּין הַכָּאָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָהּ קִצְבָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing between two kinds of beating
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב's statement shows that lashes are worse than death.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only unlimited beating is worse than death. Limited תורה מלקות is lighter, so death remains the severe matter.

steps.title: The proof only works for the רבנן, not for רבי
steps.stepSummary: רב יעקב מנהר פקוד attacks the basic proof from the pregnant woman. According to רבי, there is no death penalty in that case at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יעקב from נהר פקוד objected: This works for the רבנן, who say 'נפש' means an actual life. But according to רבי, who says it means money, what can be said?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now attacks the whole proof from the fighting men and the pregnant woman. It does not hold up according to every opinion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof needed the man to be warned for the death penalty, so that the warning would also cover lashes. According to רבי, if he killed the woman by accident he only pays money, so there is no death penalty here. Then there was no warning for lashes either, and the case proves nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: An actual life (a real death penalty)

phrases.aramaic: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַב יַעֲקֹב מִנְּהַר פְּקוֹד:
phrases.english: Rav Ya'akov from Nehar Pekod objected to this:
This works well according to the Rabbis,
who say it means an actual life,
phrases.notes: This is about 'ונתתה נפש תחת נפש' (שמות 21:23), in the case of the men fighting who hit a pregnant woman.

phrases.english: but according to Rabbi, who says it means money,
what is there to say?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַב יַעֲקֹב מִנְּהַר פְּקוֹד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns back to attack the original proof itself, not the side question of steps 1-2.
steps.kashyaTarget: The proof from the pregnant woman case that a warned person pays and is not flogged.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: According to רבי there is no death penalty in that case, so there is no 'severe warning' that could cover lashes.

steps.title: New source: the man who strikes his fellow
steps.stepSummary: In the name of רבא, רב יעקב brings a new proof from 'אם יקום והתהלך.' The attacker is held in custody. If the victim dies he is killed, and if not he pays שבת and ריפוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב יעקב from נהר פקוד said in the name of רבא: the source is from here: 'If he rises and walks outside on his staff, the striker is absolved.' Could you think the victim is walking in the market while the attacker is executed? Rather, it teaches that we hold the attacker in custody. If the victim dies, we kill the attacker. If he does not die, 'he pays for his lost work and pays for his healing.'
steps.whatsHappening: Since the old proof does not work for everyone, the גמרא brings a new source from the פסוק about someone who hits another person. This step lays out how that פסוק works, and the next steps will show why it proves our rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק cannot mean 'if the victim walks, the attacker is not executed,' because that is obvious. So it must mean that we hold the attacker until we see what happens. If the victim dies, the attacker is executed. If he recovers, he pays. This case has a real death penalty that everyone agrees on, so it avoids the problem with רבי.

keyTerms.meaning: His lost work time (payment for it)
He must pay for full healing (medical costs)

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב יַעֲקֹב מִנְּהַר פְּקוֹד
phrases.english: Rather, Rav Ya'akov from Nehar Pekod said
in the name of Rava: it is derived from here:
"If he rises and walks outside
on his staff, the one who struck him is absolved"
Could it enter your mind
that this one walks in the marketplace, and that one is executed?
Rather, it teaches that we hold him in custody,
and if the victim dies — we kill him,
and if he does not die —
"he shall pay for his lost work and have him thoroughly healed."

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב יַעֲקֹב מִנְּהַר פְּקוֹד מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרָבָא, מֵהָכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the proof that was weakened in step 3.
steps.raayaObject: That someone liable to both lashes and payment pays and is not flogged.
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמות 21:19, 'אם יקום והתהלך בחוץ על משענתו ונקה המכה... שבתו יתן ורפא ירפא'

steps.title: What is the case: was he warned?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the case is. If there was no warning, how could he be executed when the victim dies?
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If they did not warn him, why would he be executed!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up the final step of the proof. It asks whether the attacker in the פסוק was warned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A בית דין cannot execute anyone without a proper warning (התראה). The פסוק says that if the victim dies, the attacker is killed. So the case cannot be one without a warning.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? How does it look?

phrases.english: What are the circumstances?

phrases.aramaic: אִי דְּלָא אַתְרוֹ בֵּיהּ — אַמַּאי מִיקְּטִיל!
phrases.english: If they did not warn him — why would he be executed!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Clarifies the case of the פסוק so the proof can be completed.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the attacker in the פסוק received a warning.

steps.title: He was warned, yet the תורה says he pays
steps.stepSummary: Clearly he was warned. A warning for the severe punishment covers the lighter one, and still the תורה says he pays rather than getting lashes.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, clearly they warned him. Someone warned about a severe matter is warned about a light matter. And still the תורה says: 'he pays for his lost work and his healing.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the new proof. The attacker was warned, so he would normally be liable for lashes for hitting, yet the תורה makes him pay money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The warning for death (the severe matter) also counts as a warning for lashes (the light matter). So the attacker is technically liable for מלקות. But when the victim recovers, the תורה gives payment as his punishment. This shows that someone liable for both pays and is not flogged, and this proof works for everyone.

keyTerms.meaning: A light matter, the lesser punishment
The Merciful One, meaning the תורה

steps.whatToRemember: רבא's proof, reported by רב יעקב מנהר פקוד, is that the attacker in 'אם יקום והתהלך' was warned for death, which also covers lashes, yet the תורה makes him pay 'שבתו יתן ורפא ירפא.' This avoids the problem with רבי. But it is not the final word: רב אשי challenges it in steps 7-8 (step 9 answers his second challenge), and רב מרי's challenge in step 10 is left as a קשיא.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think he was not liable for lashes because he was never warned for them. The point is that he WAS effectively warned, through the death warning, and the תורה still gave him payment instead.

phrases.english: Rather, obviously they warned him,
and one who is warned for a severe matter
is warned for a light matter,
phrases.notes: The severe matter is death, and the light matter is lashes for hitting.

phrases.english: and the Merciful One said
"he shall pay for his lost work and have him thoroughly healed."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 5 and completes the proof begun in step 4.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He was warned. The death warning also covers lashes, yet the תורה requires payment, so he pays and is not flogged.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: According to this proof, someone liable for both lashes and payment pays and is not flogged, learned from 'שבתו יתן ורפא ירפא.' רב מרי's challenge in step 10 later leaves the proof as a קשיא.

steps.title: Does a warning for death count as a warning for lashes?
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי questions the rule that a warning for a severe punishment also counts as a warning for a lighter one.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי objects: How do you know that someone warned about a severe punishment counts as warned about a lighter one? Maybe he does not!
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי attacks the rule that step 6 depended on. That rule said a warning for death also covers lashes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof in step 6 worked only if the attacker had a valid warning for lashes. He was warned only about the death penalty. If that warning does not carry over to lashes, then he never could have gotten lashes, and the פסוק proves nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: strongly objects to it; a sharp challenge
one who has been given a formal warning (הַתְרָאָה) before the sin
a severe matter; here, the more severe punishment
a light matter; here, the lighter punishment

phrases.english: Rav Ashi strongly objects to it:
phrases.notes: He is going after the proof from 'אם יקום והתהלך' in step 4.

phrases.english: From where do we know that one warned about a severe matter
is considered warned about a light matter?
Perhaps he is not!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the assumption from step 6 that the warning for death covers lashes.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that a warning for a severe punishment counts as a warning for a lighter one.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the warning does not carry over, the attacker could never have gotten lashes. Then the fact that he pays proves nothing about money replacing lashes.

steps.title: Maybe lashes are worse than death
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי adds a second attack. Even if a warning carries over, maybe lashes are the more severe punishment, as רב said about חנניה, מישאל and עזריה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And even if you say a warning does carry over, how do you know death is the more severe punishment? Maybe lashes are more severe! As רב said: if they had whipped חנניה, מישאל and עזריה, they would have bowed to the idol!
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי keeps going with a second attack. Even if a warning for something severe covers something lighter, who says death is the severe one here?
steps.deeperAnalysis: If lashes are worse than death, then a warning about death would not cover lashes, since it only covers lighter things. רב's statement seems to show this: חנניה, מישאל and עזריה were ready to die in the fire, but whipping would have broken them.

keyTerms.meaning: and if you will say; even if we grant your point

steps.confusionAlert: רב is not saying lashes are a worse punishment in a court. He is talking about a beating meant to break someone, as the next step explains.

phrases.english: And if you say that he is considered warned,
from where do we know that death is more severe?
Perhaps lashes are more severe?
As Rav said:
Had they whipped Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah,
phrases.notes: Instead of throwing them into the fiery furnace (דניאל 3).

phrases.english: they would have worshipped the idol!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second layer of the same attack, granting the point of step 7 for the sake of argument.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption that death is more severe than lashes.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If lashes are more severe, a warning about death would not cover lashes. So the attacker in 'אם יקום' could not have gotten lashes, and the proof falls.

steps.title: Court lashes have a limit
steps.stepSummary: רב סמא answers: רב was talking about endless beating. Court lashes have a fixed number, so they are lighter than death.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב סמא son of רב אסי said to רב אשי (and some say רב סמא son of רב אשי said it): Don't you see a difference between beating that has a limit and beating that has no limit?
steps.whatsHappening: רב סמא answers the second part of רב אשי's attack. This is the same answer the גמרא gave earlier, now used again for the new proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Court lashes have a set number, so they really are lighter than death. רב was talking about beating with no end, which can be worse than dying. So the proof can still say death is the severe punishment.

keyTerms.meaning: and some say; a second version of who said it
a fixed limit or set amount
is there no difference to you?

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב סַמָּא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אַסִּי לְרַב אָשֵׁי,
phrases.english: Rav Samma, son of Rav Asi, said to Rav Ashi,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ רַב סַמָּא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אָשֵׁי לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: and some say it was Rav Samma, son of Rav Ashi, who said to Rav Ashi:
Is there no difference to you
between beating that has a limit
and beating that has no limit?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב סַמָּא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אַסִּי לְרַב אָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the second attack (step 8) by limiting רב's statement.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction between two kinds of beating
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב's statement shows that lashes are worse than death.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only endless beating is worse than death. Court lashes, which have a limit, are lighter.

steps.title: Maybe the פסוק is about an accidental injury
steps.stepSummary: רב מרי suggests the פסוק may be about someone who hit by accident and is cleared from גלות, not from death. If so, the proof falls. The גמרא admits this is a real difficulty.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב מרי objects: How do you know the פסוק is about someone who hit on purpose, and 'he shall be clean' means clean from execution? Maybe it is about someone who hit by accident, and 'he shall be clean' means clean from גלות! The גמרא says: this is difficult.
steps.whatsHappening: רב מרי attacks the proof itself by reading the פסוק a different way. The גמרא admits it has no answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the attacker hit by accident, there was never a warning and never any chance of lashes. Then his paying for lost work and medical costs says nothing about money replacing lashes. The proof from 'אם יקום והתהלך' is left standing on shaky ground.

keyTerms.meaning: and he shall be clean, meaning freed (from a punishment)
exile to a city of refuge, the punishment for accidental killing
it is difficult; the challenge stays unanswered

steps.whatToRemember: The proof from 'אם יקום והתהלך' is left with an unanswered קשיא. Maybe the פסוק is about an accident, where lashes never applied.

phrases.english: Rav Mari strongly objects to it:
From where do we know that it is about one who hit on purpose,
and 'he shall be clean' means clean from execution?
Perhaps it is about one who hit by accident,
and 'he shall be clean' means clean from exile?
It is difficult.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new attack on the proof itself, after רב אשי's attack was answered.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that the פסוק 'אם יקום והתהלך' is about an intentional attacker.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the פסוק is about an accident, there is no warning and no lashes at all. So it cannot show that payment replaces lashes.

steps.title: ריש לקיש: our משנה follows רבי מאיר
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש solves the original contradiction differently: our משנה follows רבי מאיר, who holds a person gets lashes and also pays.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש said: Whose opinion is this משנה? It is רבי מאיר, who says a person gets lashes and pays.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a brand-new answer to the original contradiction. Our משנה says one who violates his sister pays a fine, but the משנה in מכות says he gets lashes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the גמרא tried to show that money comes in place of lashes. ריש לקיש drops that whole approach. For רבי מאיר there is no contradiction, since both punishments apply together.

keyTerms.meaning: he gets lashes and also pays

steps.whyThisMatters: This changes the whole approach. Instead of choosing between lashes and money, the משנה follows a תנא who gives both.

phrases.english: Reish Lakish said:
Whose is this? It is Rabbi Meir,
phrases.notes: 'This' is our משנה, which makes one who violates his sister pay a fine.

phrases.english: who said: He gets lashes and pays.

steps.triggerLanguage: רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ אָמַר הָא מַנִּי רַבִּי מֵאִיר הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the earlier proofs were challenged, a completely different solution to the original contradiction is offered.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Our משנה follows רבי מאיר: a person can get lashes and also pay.

steps.title: Then even his daughter should be included
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges ריש לקיש: if the משנה follows רבי מאיר, it should also list his daughter, and it does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it is רבי מאיר, then even his daughter too!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on ריש לקיש's answer right away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If רבי מאיר makes a person pay even when he also gets a body punishment, then the משנה should also list a man who violates his daughter. But the משנה does not list her. So it seems the משנה does not follow רבי מאיר.

phrases.english: If it is Rabbi Meir,
then even his daughter too!
phrases.notes: Meaning: one who violates his own daughter should also pay the fine, but our משנה does not list her.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי רַבִּי מֵאִיר אֲפִילּוּ בִּתּוֹ נָמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly challenges ריש לקיש's answer in step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: ריש לקיש's claim that our משנה follows רבי מאיר.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: According to רבי מאיר, the fine would apply to his daughter too. Since the משנה leaves her out, it does not seem to follow רבי מאיר.

steps.title: A possible defense: רבי מאיר holds lashes and pay, but not death and pay
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests a way to save ריש לקיש: רבי מאיר holds that someone can get lashes and also pay, but not that someone can be liable to death and also pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say that רבי מאיר holds 'he gets lashes and pays,' but does not hold 'he dies and pays'...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a possible answer to the question from step 12. This is a setup, and the very next line will test it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case of a man with his own daughter carries the death penalty. If רבי מאיר only says 'lashed and pays' and not 'dies and pays,' that would explain why the daughter case is missing from the משנה. Then ריש לקיש's answer still works.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you say (a possible answer is being suggested)
He gets lashes and also pays
He is liable to death and also pays
He holds this view / he does not hold this view

phrases.english: And if you say: Rabbi Meir,
holds that one is lashed and pays,
but does not hold that one dies and pays,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a possible defense of ריש לקיש against the challenge in step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the opinion: רבי מאיר's rule applies only to lashes, not to death.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If the משנה follows רבי מאיר, it should list the daughter case too.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי מאיר holds 'lashed and pays' only, so the death-penalty daughter case does not belong in the list.

steps.title: A ברייתא shows רבי מאיר makes a person pay even when liable to death
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא where רבי מאיר requires a thief to pay four or five times even though the slaughter was on שבת or for עבודה זרה, which carry death.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does he really not hold it? But a ברייתא teaches: If someone stole and slaughtered on שבת, or stole and slaughtered for עבודה זרה, or stole an ox that was sentenced to stoning and slaughtered it, he pays four or five times. This is the view of רבי מאיר, and the חכמים exempt him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the defense from step 13. It shows a case where רבי מאיר makes someone pay even though the act carries the death penalty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Slaughtering on שבת or for עבודה זרה is a capital crime. Yet רבי מאיר still requires the payment of four or five times. That looks like 'dies and pays,' which contradicts step 13.

keyTerms.meaning: But it was taught in a ברייתא (introduces a challenge)
An ox sentenced to be stoned
Paying four or five times (four for a sheep, five for an ox)

phrases.english: And does he not? But it was taught:
If he stole and slaughtered on Shabbat,
stole and slaughtered for idolatry,
stole an ox to be stoned and slaughtered it,
he pays four or five times,
the words of Rabbi Meir, and the Sages exempt!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the defense offered in step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that רבי מאיר does not hold 'dies and pays.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In the ברייתא, the slaughter carries death, yet רבי מאיר requires payment, so he seems to hold 'dies and pays.'

steps.title: The ברייתא is about a thief whose slaughter was done by someone else
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that this ברייתא was already explained by רבי יוחנן: it speaks of a thief who had another person slaughter for him.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it was already said about this ברייתא: רבי יעקב said in the name of רבי יוחנן, and some say רבי ירמיה said in the name of ריש לקיש, and רבי אבין, רבי אילעא and the whole group said in the name of רבי יוחנן: It is talking about someone who slaughters through another person.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the proof from the ברייתא. It says the case is one where the thief did not slaughter himself; someone else did it for him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If someone else did the slaughtering, the thief himself did not break שבת or serve עבודה זרה, so he is not liable to death. He only pays. So the ברייתא is not a case of 'dies and pays,' and the defense in step 13 stands.

keyTerms.meaning: But it was already said about it
And some say (a second version of who said it)

phrases.english: But it was stated about it,

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יַעֲקֹב אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן,
phrases.english: Rabbi Yaakov said that Rabbi Yochanan said,
and some say: Rabbi Yirmeya said
that Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said,

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי אָבִין וְרַבִּי אִילְעָא וְכֹל חֲבוּרָתָא
phrases.english: Rabbi Avin and Rabbi Ila and the whole group
said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan:
It is about one who slaughters through another.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 14 by redefining the case in the ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case: the slaughter was done by an agent.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The thief slaughtered himself, so he is liable to death and still pays.
steps.terutzMaskana: Someone else slaughtered, so the thief faces no death penalty and simply pays.
steps.whyThisMatters: This keeps alive the idea that רבי מאיר holds 'lashed and pays' but not 'dies and pays,' which protects ריש לקיש's answer.

steps.title: How can one person sin and another be liable?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if the agent did the forbidden slaughter, how can the thief be made to pay for it?
steps.simpleTranslation: Can it be that this one sins and that one becomes liable?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer of step 15. If someone else did the slaughtering, why should the thief owe four or five times?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, when a person sends someone to do a sin, the sender is not responsible; the one who acted is. So it seems strange that the thief pays for a slaughter that someone else did.
steps.confusionAlert: The question is not about the death penalty. It is about the payment of four or five times: why should the thief owe it if he did not slaughter?

phrases.english: Does this one sin and that one become liable?
phrases.notes: The one who slaughtered is the agent; the one being charged is the thief who sent him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: The explanation that the ברייתא is about slaughter through another person.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A person is normally not responsible for a sin done by his agent, so the thief should not owe four or five times.

steps.title: רבא: slaughter is like selling, which always involves another person
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers from the פסוק 'and slaughters it or sells it': just as selling needs another person, slaughter through another person also counts.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: The תורה says 'and slaughters it or sells it.' Just as selling is done through another person, so too slaughter can be done through another person.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the question of step 16 with a פסוק. He shows that for this law the תורה makes the thief liable even when someone else slaughtered.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק puts slaughtering next to selling. You cannot sell without a buyer, so selling always involves another person. Since slaughter is listed together with selling, slaughter done through another person also makes the thief liable.

keyTerms.meaning: And slaughters it or sells it

phrases.english: Rava said: The Merciful One said:
"And slaughters it or sells it,"
just as selling is through another,
so too slaughter is through another.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 16 with a source from the פסוק.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Special Torah rule learned from a פסוק that puts slaughter next to selling.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A thief cannot be liable for slaughter done by his agent.
steps.terutzMaskana: For four-or-five payment, the תורה makes the thief liable even when another person slaughtered.

steps.title: Two other sources: the words 'or' and 'instead of'
steps.stepSummary: The school of רבי ישמעאל learns the agent rule from the word 'או', and the school of חזקיה learns it from the word 'תחת'.
steps.simpleTranslation: The school of רבי ישמעאל taught: 'Or' comes to include the agent. The school of חזקיה taught: 'Instead of' comes to include the agent.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings two more sources for the same rule that the thief is liable when his agent slaughters. Each one learns it from a different word in the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא learned the rule from comparing slaughter to selling. These two schools reach the same rule from extra words: 'או' (or) and 'תחת' (instead of). The conclusion is the same: the agent's slaughter counts against the thief.

keyTerms.meaning: Agent, a messenger who acts for someone

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא about stealing and slaughtering is about a thief whose agent slaughtered. The thief faces no death penalty, so it does not prove רבי מאיר holds 'dies and pays.' The תורה makes the thief liable through his agent here, learned from 'slaughters or sells,' from 'או,' or from 'תחת.'

phrases.english: The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught:
"Or" comes to include the agent.
The school of Chizkiya taught:
"Instead of" comes to include the agent.
phrases.notes: This is the word from the end of the same פסוק: he pays five cattle 'instead of' the ox.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives other sources for the same answer that רבא gave.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Other sources from extra words in the same פסוק.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Without a special source, the thief would not be liable for his agent's act.
steps.terutzMaskana: The words 'או' or 'תחת' teach that the agent's slaughter makes the thief liable.

steps.title: מר זוטרא asks how an agent can create liability the thief himself would not have
steps.stepSummary: מר זוטרא challenges the idea that the thief pays when an agent slaughters, since he would not pay if he slaughtered himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר זוטרא objected: Is there anything where, if a person does it himself, he is not liable, but if his agent does it, he is liable?
steps.whatsHappening: מר זוטרא attacks the explanation from steps 15-17, which says the thief pays because his agent slaughtered.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the thief slaughters on שבת himself, he does not pay. So it seems strange that sending an agent should make him pay more than doing it himself. Normally an agent stands in for the sender, so he should not create a stronger obligation than the sender's own act.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who raises the challenge
Agent, someone acting on another's behalf

phrases.english: Mar Zutra objected to this:
Is there any matter
where if he himself did it, he is not liable,
phrases.notes: He means the thief slaughtering on שבת himself, who does not pay the four or five.

phrases.english: yet if an agent does it, he is liable?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the agent explanation that steps 15-18 established and supported from פסוקים.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that the thief pays four or five when an agent slaughters on שבת
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An agent cannot make the sender liable for something the sender would not be liable for if he did it himself.

steps.title: The thief is spared only because he gets the bigger punishment
steps.stepSummary: The thief's own slaughter does make him liable to pay; he is spared only because of the rule of קם ליה בדרבה מיניה.
steps.simpleTranslation: When he does it himself, he is not exempt because he isn't liable. Rather, he is exempt because he receives the greater punishment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers מר זוטרא: a thief who slaughters himself really is liable to pay. He is let off only because he receives the death penalty for שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule of קם ליה בדרבה מיניה means that when one act brings both death and money, only the bigger punishment is given. With an agent, the thief himself did not break שבת, so there is no death penalty for him, and the payment comes back.

keyTerms.meaning: He receives the greater punishment, so he is exempt from the lesser one

steps.confusionAlert: The thief is not 'not liable' for the slaughter. He is liable, but the payment is pushed aside by the death penalty. Once the death penalty is gone, as in the agent case, the payment stands.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that קם ליה בדרבה מיניה only sets aside the smaller penalty. It does not cancel the obligation.

phrases.english: He himself is exempt not because he is not liable,

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא מִשּׁוּם דְּקָם לֵיהּ בִּדְרַבָּה מִינֵּיהּ.
phrases.english: but because he receives the greater punishment.
phrases.notes: The greater punishment is the death penalty for breaking שבת.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיהוּ, לָאו מִשּׁוּם דְּלָא מִיחַיַּיב, אֶלָּא מִשּׁוּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers מר זוטרא's challenge directly.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The thief who slaughters himself has no payment obligation at all, so an agent should not create one.
steps.terutzMaskana: The obligation exists in both cases. Only the death penalty blocks it, and that penalty is missing when an agent slaughters.

steps.title: Why do the רבנן exempt the thief in the agent case?
steps.stepSummary: If the ברייתא speaks of an agent, there is no death penalty, so why do the רבנן exempt the thief from paying?
steps.simpleTranslation: If the case is one who slaughtered through another person, what is the reason of the רבנן who exempt him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to רבי יוחנן's reading of the ברייתא and now questions the other side, the רבנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 20 showed that in the agent case the thief gets no death penalty, so he should pay. Yet the רבנן in the ברייתא exempt him, and that needs a reason.

keyTerms.meaning: The Sages who disagree with רבי מאיר

phrases.english: If it is a case of one who slaughtered through another,
what is the reason of the Rabbis who exempt him?
phrases.notes: These are the רבנן in the ברייתא from step 14 who argue with רבי מאיר.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי בְּטוֹבֵחַ עַל יְדֵי אַחֵר, מַאי טַעְמַיְיהוּ דְּרַבָּנַן דְּפָטְרִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on step 20. Since the agent case has no death penalty, the רבנן's exemption is now hard to explain.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's explanation of the ברייתא as an agent case
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: With an agent there is no death penalty, so nothing should exempt the thief, yet the רבנן exempt him.

steps.title: The גמרא begins by asking who these חכמים are
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens its answer by identifying which חכמים argue with רבי מאיר.
steps.simpleTranslation: Who are the חכמים?
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא starts its answer by asking who the חכמים are, and the full answer comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא does not give a reason right away. It plans to explain the exemption by showing who these חכמים are and what view they hold.

phrases.english: Who are the Sages?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the answer to step 21's question about the רבנן.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Identifies the opinion holder (the answer continues next)
